title: Industrial and Product Design
description: How designers frame a problem, fit products to bodies and processes, test with people and weigh the choices.
audience: Curious adults with school maths. No drawing or software skills needed.
outcomes: You'll be able to write a need, not a solution.
You'll be able to use percentiles, Fitts and Hick in a design decision.
You'll be able to judge a part for moulding and assembly.
You'll be able to compare concepts and lifetimes with numbers.

NASA-STD-3000 Man-Systems Integration Standards, Vol. I section 3 (anthropometry and biomechanics)

lessons.title: Problems before products
lessons.objective: Turn a vague request into a problem statement and a list of needs, separate from solutions.

concepts.title: Design brief
concepts.summary: A short statement of who the product is for, what they need to do, and the limits it must fit.

concepts.title: Need versus solution
concepts.summary: A need says what must happen; a solution says how. Mixing them early closes off better ideas.

misconceptions: Learners start with a product (a better kettle) rather than a person doing something (making a hot drink).
Learners write requirements that smuggle in a solution, such as 'has a lid hinge'.
Learners think the design process is a straight line. Teams widen and narrow twice, then loop.
sequence: Take 'design a better kettle'. Ask who, doing what, where, and what goes wrong.
Sort statements into needs and solutions.
Rewrite a solution as the need behind it.
Show the Double Diamond: discover, define, develop, deliver.
Put in numbers: capacity, time, price, safety limit.
Finish with a one-sentence problem statement.
examples: 'Lid hinges at the back' is a solution; the need is 'pour without the lid falling onto the hand'.
'Boil 1 litre in under 3 minutes' is a measurable requirement.
A cold-chain delivery bag: the real need is food kept below 5 C for 2 hours, not an insulated bag.

figures.shows: Eight statements about a kettle, each drawn on a card.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each to Need or Solution.

figures.shows: Double Diamond with four phases labelled by verbs and a marker between diamonds.
figures.learnerAction: Tap a phase to see its typical outputs.

historyNotes: The Design Council published the Double Diamond in 2005, based on earlier work of the British Design Council and the divergence-convergence model of Banathy (1996).

lessons.title: Affordances, signifiers and mapping
lessons.objective: Tell what a design signals, match controls to results and distinguish slips from mistakes.

concepts.title: Signifier
concepts.summary: A perceivable cue that tells the user what an action does and where to do it.

concepts.title: Mapping
concepts.summary: The relationship between controls and what they affect; natural mapping uses spatial layout.

misconceptions: Learners treat 'affordance' and 'signifier' as the same. An affordance is what is possible; a signifier shows it.
Learners blame the user for errors that the design invites.
Learners think labels fix poor mapping.
sequence: A door that people push when they should pull.
Affordance vs signifier.
Mapping with a four-burner stove.
Feedback: what happens after the action.
Slips (right goal, wrong action) vs mistakes (wrong goal).
Constraints and defaults.
examples: Four knobs in a row for a 2x2 stove: 4! = 24 possible mappings, 1 natural.
A flat plate on a door signals push; a handle signals pull.
Pressing the wrong adjacent key is a slip; setting the oven to the wrong temperature because the recipe is unclear is a mistake.

figures.learnerAction: Choose which action each invites.

figures.shows: Stove knob layouts and the number of mappings.
figures.learnerAction: Predict which layout leads to errors.

lessons.title: Designing to bodies
lessons.objective: Use percentiles to set dimensions, and the NIOSH limit to judge a lift.

concepts.title: Percentile
concepts.summary: The 95th percentile is the size that 95 percent of people are at or below; for a normal distribution it is the mean plus 1.645 standard deviations.

concepts.title: Design for the range
concepts.summary: Clearances use the large end, reaches use the small end, and adjustable features cover the span.

misconceptions: Learners design for the average person; almost nobody is average in every dimension.
Learners use the 95th percentile for everything. Reach and force limits need the 5th.
Learners add percentiles of different dimensions; body parts are correlated imperfectly.
sequence: Variation among people.
Mean and standard deviation; normal curve.
5th and 95th percentile: mean -/+ 1.645 SD.
Clearance (large) vs reach (small).
Adjustable range.
Lifting: the recommended weight limit starts at 23 kg and shrinks with multipliers.
examples: Illustrative stature: mean 1750 mm, SD 70 mm. 95th: 1750+1.645*70=1865 mm; 5th: 1635 mm.
A doorway to clear the 95th percentile with 100 mm margin: 1965 mm.
RWL = 23 x 0.8 x 0.9 = 16.56 kg; a 20 kg lift gives a lifting index of 1.21, above 1.0.

figures.shows: Normal curve of stature with draggable percentile marks.
figures.learnerAction: Move the mark to see the share of people covered.

figures.shows: Person silhouettes at 5th and 95th percentile at a counter and a shelf.
figures.learnerAction: Move a shelf up and down and see who can reach.

questionPlan.sample: Mean 1750 mm, SD 70 mm. 95th percentile in mm, to the nearest mm?

historyNotes: Henry Dreyfuss's Designing for People (1955) popularised the use of human measurement ('Joe and Josephine') in design.

lessons.title: Controls, displays and the cost of choice
lessons.objective: Predict pointing time with Fitts's law and choice time with Hick's law.

concepts.title: Fitts's law
concepts.summary: Movement time grows with log2(D/W + 1), where D is distance and W target width (Shannon form).

concepts.title: Hick's law
concepts.summary: Choice time grows with log2(n + 1) for n equally likely options.

misconceptions: Learners think smaller controls are always neater; they cost time and errors.
Learners think more options always help; each doubles roughly one step.
Learners ignore the edges of a screen, which act as infinitely deep targets.
sequence: Pointing is a task with a distance and a target width.
Index of difficulty ID = log2(D/W + 1) in bits.
Movement time MT = a + b ID with constants fitted to a device.
Halving the width adds about one bit.
Hick: choice time grows with log2(n + 1).
Design moves: bigger, closer, fewer, grouped.
examples: D=160 mm, W=20 mm: ID=log2(9)=3.17 bits. With a=0.1 s, b=0.15 s/bit: MT=0.58 s.
W=10 mm: ID=log2(17)=4.09 bits, MT=0.71 s.
Menu of 7 items with b=0.2 s: 0.2*log2(8)=0.6 s; 15 items: 0.8 s.

figures.shows: Movement time against index of difficulty as a straight line.
figures.learnerAction: Drag distance and width to move the point.

figures.shows: A row of buttons with a cursor path and a width slider.
figures.learnerAction: Resize the target and watch the predicted time update.

questionPlan.sample: D=160, W=20. ID in bits to 2 decimals (Shannon form)?

historyNotes: Paul Fitts published his law in 1954; William Hick published his choice-reaction result in 1952.

lessons.title: Designing for everyone
lessons.objective: Apply universal design principles and read accessibility dimensions.

concepts.title: Universal design
concepts.summary: Design usable by as many people as possible without adaptation, set out in seven principles.

concepts.title: Access dimensions
concepts.summary: Reach range 380 to 1220 mm, door clear width at least 815 mm, ramp slope at most 1:12.

misconceptions: Learners treat accessibility as a special feature for a minority. Many users benefit: parents with prams, injured people, tired people.
Learners think a ramp slope of 1:12 is steep; it is the maximum.
Learners think 'average user' covers everyone.
sequence: Ability varies over a lifetime and in a day.
The seven principles in one line each.
Reach range numbers.
Ramp 1:12 means 1 unit rise per 12 along.
Door clearances and turning circle of 1525 mm.
Cost of retrofit versus design in.
examples: Rise of 0.6 m needs a 7.2 m ramp at 1:12.
Forward reach 380 to 1220 mm: a socket at 300 mm fails and a switch at 1500 mm fails.
Door clear width 815 mm is 32 inches.

figures.shows: Wheelchair user silhouette against a counter with the reach band shaded.
figures.learnerAction: Move a socket and switch up and down.

figures.shows: Seven principles with example products.
figures.learnerAction: Match product to principle.

questionPlan.sample: Rise 0.6 m at slope 1:12. Ramp length in m?

historyNotes: Ronald Mace coined 'universal design' and led the group that published the seven principles in 1997.

lessons.title: Form, function and a short history
lessons.objective: Place landmark designs in time and say what each idea in 'form follows function' meant.

concepts.title: Form follows function
concepts.summary: The phrase from architect Louis Sullivan (1896) says form should come from purpose, not decoration.

concepts.title: Rams's principles
concepts.summary: Dieter Rams's ten principles of good design, among them that good design is as little design as possible.

misconceptions: Learners think 'form follows function' means plain. It means form should arise from use.
Learners think design history is a list of styles; each is a response to materials and production.
Learners think industrial design began with computers.
sequence: Craft to industry: bent beech chairs (Thonet No. 14, 1859).
The phrase and its source (1896).
Bauhaus (1919): design for production.
Mid-century: moulded plywood (Eames, 1946), Braun radio SK 4 (1956).
Rams's principles.
Form language today: grouping, radii, colour, material, finish.
examples: Timeline: 1859 Thonet No. 14; 1896 Sullivan; 1919 Bauhaus; 1932 Anglepoise lamp; 1946 Eames moulded plywood chairs; 1956 Braun SK 4; 2007 first iPhone.
Thonet No. 14 packs 36 disassembled chairs in a 1 m cube.
Rams: 'less, but better'.

figures.learnerAction: Place each product on the timeline before it is revealed.

figures.shows: Four design movements as cards.
figures.learnerAction: Order them by date.

historyNotes: Thonet No. 14 was introduced in 1859; the Bauhaus was founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919; Sullivan's phrase appeared in an 1896 essay; Braun SK 4 was designed by Dieter Rams and Hans Gugelot in 1956.

lessons.title: Designing for the process
lessons.objective: Apply moulding rules (wall, draft, ribs) and see how process limits shape form.

concepts.title: Draft angle
concepts.summary: A slight taper on faces parallel to mould opening so the part releases.

concepts.title: Uniform wall
concepts.summary: Even wall thickness avoids sink marks and warping as the plastic cools evenly.

misconceptions: Learners expect that any shape drawn can be made.
Learners add thick sections for strength; cooling makes sinks and voids. Ribs do the job.
Learners forget undercuts that lock the part in the mould.
sequence: A mould opens in one direction, so every face must release.
Add a slight draft on faces parallel to the opening.
Keep walls even; core out thick regions.
Add ribs about 0.6 of the wall thickness instead of thick sections.
Place the parting line and avoid undercuts.
Round corners to ease flow and stress.
examples: Draft 1 degree on a 40 mm face moves it 40*tan1=0.70 mm.
Wall 2.5 mm: rib thickness about 1.5 mm.
A 10 mm solid boss cooled with a 2 mm wall will show a sink mark on the visible face.

figures.shows: Moulded part cross-section with wall, rib, boss and draft marked.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle each defect and see its cause.

lessons.title: Fewer parts, easier assembly
lessons.objective: Count the minimum parts and compute an assembly efficiency.

concepts.title: Theoretical minimum parts
concepts.summary: A part needs to be separate only if it moves, is a different material, or must be removed for assembly or service.

concepts.title: DFA index
concepts.summary: Efficiency = 3 s x minimum parts / actual assembly time.

misconceptions: Learners think fewer parts means weaker product; a single moulding with a snap fit can be stronger than a screwed assembly.
Learners think cheaper parts make a cheaper product; assembly labour dominates.
Learners forget serviceability.
sequence: Every part costs handling, orientation and joining.
Three questions for each part.
Minimum part count.
DFA index.
Snap fits, self-locating features, one direction of assembly.
Counterexample: serviceability and recycling.
examples: Product with 12 parts needs only 5 separate parts: a 7-part reduction.
Minimum 4 parts, assembly time 48 s: index 3*4/48=0.25.
After redesign the time is 24 s: 0.50.

figures.learnerAction: Tick the three questions per part.

lessons.title: Prototypes and user tests
lessons.objective: Choose a prototype fidelity and compute what a small test will find.

concepts.title: Fidelity
concepts.summary: How closely a prototype resembles the final product in the aspects being tested.

concepts.title: Problem discovery
concepts.summary: If each user finds a fraction p of problems, n users find 1-(1-p)^n of them.

misconceptions: Learners think five users is enough in total; it is enough per round for the common problems.
Learners polish prototypes before testing.
Learners ask opinions rather than watching behaviour.
sequence: Prototype to answer a question.
Fidelity ladder: sketch, cardboard, 3D print, working.
Observing, not asking.
Discovery model with p=0.31.
Several short rounds beat one long one.
Count errors, time and hesitation.
examples: Cardboard handle mock-up tests grip comfort for pennies.
Three rounds of five beat one round of fifteen.

historyNotes: Nielsen and Landauer's 1993 model gave p of about 31 percent as the average across the projects they studied.

lessons.title: Product life and its footprint
lessons.objective: Compare products by lifetime footprint and say how repair and durability change it.

concepts.title: Life-cycle assessment
concepts.summary: Counting the effects of a product from raw materials through use to end of life.

concepts.title: Annualised footprint
concepts.summary: Footprint over the whole life divided by years of use.

misconceptions: Learners think recycling is the main lever; making less and lasting longer matter more.
Learners think the use phase is always small; for many appliances it dominates.
Learners compare per-unit manufacture only.
sequence: Follow a product from raw material to disposal in five stages.
Find where most of the impact sits: the hotspot.
Annualise: total footprint divided by years of use.
Compare a cheap short-lived product with a durable one.
Repair, modularity and upgrade extend life.
State assumptions, since the answer changes with them.
examples: A: 50 kg CO2e to make, 20 kg per year in use, 5 years: (50+100)/5=30 kg a year.
B: 80 kg to make, 20 kg per year, 10 years: (80+200)/10=28 kg a year.
Where the use phase dominates, efficiency beats lighter materials.

lessons.title: Choosing between concepts
lessons.objective: Rank concepts with a weighted matrix and test whether the answer is robust.

concepts.title: Weighted matrix
concepts.summary: Scores times weights, summed, to compare concepts against the same criteria.

concepts.title: Sensitivity
concepts.summary: Changing the weights to see if the winner changes.

misconceptions: Learners treat the total as truth; it is a way to discuss assumptions.
Learners include criteria that all concepts satisfy equally.
Learners set weights after seeing the scores.
sequence: Turn the brief into four to six criteria.
Give each criterion a weight; weights sum to 1.
Score each concept 1 to 5 on each criterion.
Multiply and sum.
Change the weights and see if the winner changes.
Choose, and record why.
examples: Criteria: cost, ergonomics, manufacture, sustainability.
